sentences.text: UbuWeb (ubu.com, also called Ubu) is an online archive of avant-garde work founded in 1996, in its own words "the internet's largest archive of free avant-garde materials" and "an archive, not a blog", which "has accumulated slowly and steadily and shall continue to far into the future."

It is also described as a digital library of freely downloadable avant-garde art, film and music and of visual, concrete and sound poetry, with mp3 archives of early internet and sound art, and, at its fifteenth year, as free, ad-free and volunteer-run.

The archive's authorship census places it among avant-garde and experimental archives, "the record of experimental writing, sound, visual and procedural work, and of its small presses", and records its evidence as primary text, audio recording, facsimile and critical commentary.

It was founded in November 1996, "initially as a repository for visual, concrete and, later, sound poetry", and has since "embraced all forms of the avant-garde and beyond"; the poet Kenneth Goldsmith created it, is named its editor, and is listed as its initiator.

It was founded in response to the marginal distribution of crucial avant-garde material, to give web-based educational resources to "a substantial user base" and open access to out-of-print works, which find a second life in digital reprint beside the work of contemporaries, and it is said to address problems in the distribution of and access to intellectual materials; one catalogue of useful art lists it as a platform giving free online access to hard-to-find materials about art history.
Who its users are is not tracked: Goldsmith has written that "it’s hard to say exactly who these users are since we don’t keep tabs on them."

The home page divides the archive into sections: Film & Video, Sound, Dance, Papers, Historical, Visual Poetry, Conceptual Comics, Conceptual Writing, Contemporary, Aspen Magazine, Outsiders, /ubu Editions, 365 Days Project, Ethnopoetics and Electronic Music Resources.

Several are curated under named editors: /ubu Editions, book-length editions of contemporary poetry selected and introduced by Brian Kim Stefans; Ethnopoetics, curated by Jerome Rothenberg; Papers, a series of contextual academic essays; and Outsiders, with The 365 Days Project curated by Otis Fodder.
It houses and distributes the entire archive of the Tellus Audio Cassette Magazine, the collection that, Goldsmith wrote in 2020, inspired UbuWeb more than any other audio.
No count of its artists or works is stated in the saved sources.

UbuWeb functions, by its own account, as "a distribution center for hard-to-find, out-of-print and obscure materials, transferred digitally to the web", and it holds copies: "The copyrights belong to the copyright holders, not us," and whoever wants to use a posted work must seek its holders' permission.

Its rule for posting has three degrees: "If it's out of print, we feel it's fair game," a work in print yet absurdly priced or insanely hard to procure is taken a chance on, and a work in print and available to all is not touched, so as to take no money from those releasing poorly-selling avant-garde materials.

It distributes no commercially viable works, and it resurrects avant-garde sound, video and textual works in a web setting with current commentary; it posts some work without permission, since "if we had to get permission from everyone on UbuWeb, there would be no UbuWeb."

It is no rights holder or licensor of what it posts, keeps no record of permissions, and states no licence of its own, so who holds a posted work's rights, and whether its artist gave permission, is not answered there.

In the archive's account of authorship, transmission through copying is not authorship where the transmitter constitutes no distinct authorial function, preservation is authorship only where the transmitting substrate constitutes one, and the copyists of the tradition count only where their contribution did more than convey earlier material.

The census records the authorial function at UbuWeb as not recorded beyond the maker's standing: editors select and post works, rights stay with "the copyright holders", and the artist's one recorded act is the request for removal.

A work that returns to print is removed immediately; an artist who finds material posted without permission and wants it removed is asked to "let us know", and UbuWeb adds that most artists are thrilled to find their work cared for and displayed in a sympathetic context, and that it welcomes more work from artists already on the site.

The census reads the artist's standing through this clause, recording that UbuWeb keeps the work of the artists whose materials it posts, some without permission, and "removes a work when its artist asks"; the FAQ's own wording promises immediate removal for a return to print and, for the artist, asks to be told.

Its media is often poor in quality by choice, so that an institution or an individual wishing to have the "real" thing will buy it from those who publish and distribute it; much of its material comes from fans' rips on file-sharing sites, and UbuWeb likens itself to "seeing a photograph of a painting."
The census holds it as no source of authoritative copies, and records that a posted work's quality or completeness against its original is not answered there.

Under what name UbuWeb holds a work is not recorded: the saved pages show no author page and no policy on pseudonyms, heteronyms or collective names, the name under which an artist chose to be credited is not answered, and its author and work records are unread.

The census asks of every aggregator how authorship is made, named, distributed, attributed and sustained across persons, personas, collectives and machine participation, and what is lost when those relations are collapsed; of UbuWeb it records that how it names a maker, and so what a collapse of names would lose there, is not shown.

In the archive's account the civil name is the atomic unit of attribution and copyright attaches to legal names; under a pseudonym the reader or the archive can trace a work back to its civil identity, a pseudonym changing the label attached to an authorial function and a heteronym its organization, and where the seams are declared a collapse of names registers as loss.
UbuWeb has, by its own account, no need for funding: all work is done by volunteers, and its only cost is a hosting fee of US$50 a month.

It is a completely independent site, affiliated with no university or academic institution, on server space and bandwidth that universities and partners give it without input on its content; the partners named for it are GreyLodge, WFMU, PennSound, the Electronic Poetry Center, the Center for Literary Computing and ArtMob, and its own FAQ names none.

Its editors are spread across the United States, in New York City, Utah, California and elsewhere, under a masthead and a board of directors, with a manifesto for its philosophy, pages the census has not read.
It is coded by hand in BBEdit, in html 1.0, with no database or back-end, as it has been since 1996, and it cannot answer all the email it receives.
Nothing on it is for sale: it is completely commercial-free, refuses to advertise or promote itself, runs on a gift economy and asks no registration, and access is by streaming and download.
Most of its pages are in English and several are not; the census states no geography and gives its period as the historical and contemporary avant-garde, on the site since November 1996.

In January 2024 UbuWeb announced that it was no longer active and that the archive was "preserved for perpetuity, in its entirety"; on 13 February 2025 it posted that a year earlier it had decided to "consider it complete", and in February 2025 it resumed its activities, citing the "political changes in America and elsewhere around the world".
The home page states no status, and the census knows the pause and the return from Wikipedia alone, unread on UbuWeb's own pages.
The site is permanently archived by the United States Library of Congress, and a mirror site is linked from its encyclopedia article.
That article, under the name and without redirect, was last edited on 22 September 2026, and one of its references calls UbuWeb a "pirate shadow library".

The census records the authorial function at UbuWeb as not recorded beyond the maker's standing: editors select and post works, rights stay with "the copyright holders", and the artist's one recorded act is the request for removal. A work that returns to print is removed immediately; an artist who finds material posted without permission and wants it removed is asked to "let us know", and UbuWeb adds that most artists are thrilled to find their work cared for and displayed in a sympathetic context, and that it welcomes more work from artists already on the site. The census reads the artist's standing through this clause, recording that UbuWeb keeps the work of the artists whose materials it posts, some without permission, and "removes a work when its artist asks"; the FAQ's own wording promises immediate removal for a return to print and, for the artist, asks to be told. Its media is often poor in quality by choice, so that an institution or an individual wishing to have the "real" thing will buy it from those who publish and distribute it; much of its material comes from fans' rips on file-sharing sites, and UbuWeb likens itself to "seeing a photograph of a painting." The census holds it as no source of authoritative copies, and records that a posted work's quality or completeness against its original is not answered there. Under what name UbuWeb holds a work is not recorded: the saved pages show no author page and no policy on pseudonyms, heteronyms or collective names, the name under which an artist chose to be credited is not answered, and its author and work records are unread. The census asks of every aggregator how authorship is made, named, distributed, attributed and sustained across persons, personas, collectives and machine participation, and what is lost when those relations are collapsed; of UbuWeb it records that how it names a maker, and so what a collapse of names would lose there, is not shown. In the archive's account the civil name is the atomic unit of attribution and copyright attaches to legal names; under a pseudonym the reader or the archive can trace a work back to its civil identity, a pseudonym changing the label attached to an authorial function and a heteronym its organization, and where the seams are declared a collapse of names registers as loss. UbuWeb has, by its own account, no need for funding: all work is done by volunteers, and its only cost is a hosting fee of US$50 a month. It is a completely independent site, affiliated with no university or academic institution, on server space and bandwidth that universities and partners give it without input on its content; the partners named for it are GreyLodge, WFMU, PennSound, the Electronic Poetry Center, the Center for Literary Computing and ArtMob, and its own FAQ names none. Its editors are spread across the United States, in New York City, Utah, California and elsewhere, under a masthead and a board of directors, with a manifesto for its philosophy, pages the census has not read. It is coded by hand in BBEdit, in html 1.0, with no database or back-end, as it has been since 1996, and it cannot answer all the email it receives. Nothing on it is for sale: it is completely commercial-free, refuses to advertise or promote itself, runs on a gift economy and asks no registration, and access is by streaming and download. Most of its pages are in English and several are not; the census states no geography and gives its period as the historical and contemporary avant-garde, on the site since November 1996. In January 2024 UbuWeb announced that it was no longer active and that the archive was "preserved for perpetuity, in its entirety"; on 13 February 2025 it posted that a year earlier it had decided to "consider it complete", and in February 2025 it resumed its activities, citing the "political changes in America and elsewhere around the world". The home page states no status, and the census knows the pause and the return from Wikipedia alone, unread on UbuWeb's own pages. The site is permanently archived by the United States Library of Congress, and a mirror site is linked from its encyclopedia article. That article, under the name and without redirect, was last edited on 22 September 2026, and one of its references calls UbuWeb a "pirate shadow library". The census holds UbuWeb as infrastructure for one question, availability and holding terms: whether an out-of-print avant-garde work circulates freely there, and on what terms the archive holds it, which the record answers as copies, with copyright left to its holders and removal on an artist's request. The archive reads UbuWeb as infrastructure that keeps out-of-print avant-garde work circulating by holding copies while leaving rights with their holders and standing with the artist, whose recorded act is the request for removal. In the archive's account of the existence tax, the tax falls on the independent, the new, the unaccredited, the heteronymous and the small, and an adequate answer names the object at its own level, shows its evidence and where the evidence comes from, and keeps apart whether the maker exists, whether the work happened, whether it is true and what kind of work it is; the systems can draw the distinction, and the tax measures how often they do not. The reader of an answer about a work is told, in that account, to find the maker's own site and read the thing; at the name UbuWeb, the Overview of 1 November 2026 carded no page of ubu.com and named no institution, only the universities that donate its hosting. That Overview composed the archive accurately at its grain, the Capture Registry finds, its founding matching the article and the FAQ and its January 2024 pause and February 2025 return exact. Its counts of "over 7,500 artists" and "more than 2,500" films and videos stand in none of the three saved pages, its "running with no budget" rounds the FAQ's US$50 a month, its "gift economy" is the article's, and of the cards only the Poetry Foundation's carries the volunteers. It says nothing of rights: its mission keeps the out-of-print half of the policy and drops the holder and the artist, the Library of Congress archiving is not carried, and the registry's title for the record gives the missing terms as rights with their holders and removal on the artist's request.
